answer.sourceLine: Planck’s answer to James Murphy in “Epilogue: A Socratic Dialogue. Planck–Einstein–Murphy,” in Where Is Science Going? (New York: W. W. Norton, 1932), p. 217. The edition credits the translation to James Murphy. The popular wording matches the printed English text word for word.

source.heading: Where the line actually appears

docMeta.dd: Epilogue: A Socratic Dialogue. Planck–Einstein–Murphy, p. 217
New York: W. W. Norton & Company, 1932 (First Edition), with a prologue by Albert Einstein
“Translation and biographical note by James Murphy” (title page)

source.excerpt:
MURPHY: You have often said that the progress of science consists in the discovery of a new mystery the moment one thinks that something fundamental has been solved. …

PLANCK: As to the first point, that about the discovery of new mysteries. This is undoubtedly true. Science cannot solve the ultimate mystery of nature. And that is because, in the last analysis, we ourselves are part of nature and therefore part of the mystery that we are trying to solve. Music and art are, to an extent, also attempts to solve or at least to express the mystery. But to my mind the more we progress with either the more we are brought into harmony with all nature itself. And that is one of the great services of science to the individual.
trail: The exact sentence is on p. 217 of the 1932 Norton first edition, in Planck’s reply to Murphy (Internet Archive full text ↗).
Wikiquote’s sourced quotes for Planck list it under Where is Science Going? (1932), “Epilogue, p. 217,” along with two shorter variants (Wikiquote: Max Planck ↗).
The Marginalian also quotes the line and says it comes from the Socratic dialogue with Einstein at the end of the 1932 book (The Marginalian ↗).

author.name: Max Planck
author.heading: About Max Planck
author.metaLine: 1858–1947 · German theoretical physicist, founder of quantum theory
author.bio: Max Karl Ernst Ludwig Planck was the German physicist whose work on energy quanta launched quantum theory. He won the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics. In his later years he wrote and lectured widely on causality, free will and how science relates to religion. Where Is Science Going? (1932) collects that thinking for English readers.

misattribution.heading: Real quote, loosely copied
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct. What drifts online is the wording, and the setting the line is said to come from.

items.who: “…we ourselves are a part of the mystery that we are trying to solve”
items.why: This common variant drops “of nature and therefore part.” In the 1932 text, Planck first says we are part of nature and only then part of the mystery. Wikiquote lists this form as a variant (Wikiquote ↗).

items.who: “…for in the final analysis we ourselves are part of the mystery we are trying to solve”
items.why: This variant merges the two sentences into one and changes “last analysis” to “final analysis.” That wording is not in the 1932 English edition. Wikiquote lists it as a variant (Wikiquote ↗).
Einstein is one of the three speakers in the book’s closing dialogue, but Planck is not answering him here. He is answering a question from James Murphy, the book’s translator (1932 text, p. 217 ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The full popular wording matches Planck’s reply on p. 217 of Where Is Science Going? (Norton, 1932) word for word (Internet Archive ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Where Is Science Going? was published in 1932, when quantum theory was challenging the old idea of strict causality. The book ends with a “Socratic dialogue” between Planck, Einstein and James Murphy. In this exchange, Murphy brings up Planck’s often-repeated view that every scientific advance uncovers a new mystery. Planck agrees, and explains why: the scientist is part of what he is studying.
He goes straight on to music and art. He calls them attempts “to solve or at least to express the mystery,” and says that progress in either brings us “into harmony with all nature itself.”
